summary: Observing a bright point at sunrise with a telescope.
description: In 2010, a witness reported an old sighting made using an Admiral 1000 telescope (15x-60x zoom) borrowed from a friend. Two other people present at the time also observed the phenomenon. On Wednesday, October 8, 1969, at 7:10 a.m., three people were drawn to a bright point in the sky. The witness then observed, through the telescope, an object moving slowly from north to south in a back-and-forth motion. He described a disk accompanied by two satellites orbiting the main object. The observation lasted about twenty minutes. The witness paused briefly but saw nothing upon returning. No other reports concerning a phenomenon seen in October 1969 in the region or surrounding areas were collected by GEIPAN. Observing a bright point in the morning sky is in itself a common occurrence: it could, in this case, be Sirius or a weather balloon. The object's disappearance was also quite commonplace: the increasing brightness of the sky at sunrise rendered it invisible. The observation through the telescope, as enthusiastically described by the witness, is more unusual (satellites orbiting the object); however, zoom telescopes are known to be very susceptible to optical aberrations (flare that causes ghost images); the witness claims that this telescope was of good quality without any noticeable defects, since he had previously been able to observe Jupiter's moons. The age and unique nature of the testimony, along with the inability to verify the quality of this telescope, prevent us from making a definitive judgment on this testimony: classification "C".
